entries.subject: Archive access and query interface
entries.finding: The ESO archive serves this telescope. Its TAP service answered anonymously on 2026-09-17, and ESO states that without authenticating any user can download public files, raw or reduced; proprietary files need a User Portal login. The same services (TAP, calselector trees, header service, data portal) already drive this repository's VLTI calibrations.
entries.revisitWhen: A body or star in this repository needs data from this telescope.

entries.subject: Proprietary period, licence and credit
entries.finding: ESO archive data are proprietary for typically one year, set by programme type rather than by telescope, and public survey raw data carry none. Public data are distributed under CC BY 4.0 ("All data in the ESO archive retain ESO's copyright, and are distributed according to the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license"), and a paper or cast body credits ESO with the programme identifier, or the archive DOI for processed data.
entries.revisitWhen: This facility's data are used, or its terms are needed for a derived product.

entries.subject: Reduction software
entries.finding: No WFI, FEROS or GROND pipeline appears in ESO's pipeline table or FTP index. FEROS is reduced by a MIDAS-based system at La Silla, and GROND's pipeline belongs to MPE, whose page states GROND data are not public. No licence statement is published on ESO's pipeline pages; the only licence text found on an ESO server is a GPL-2-or-later header in a Common Pipeline Library source file.
entries.revisitWhen: Raw data from this facility are reduced here.

entries.subject: What this archive holds for catalogued bodies
entries.finding: A name screen of all 498 catalogued bodies against the ESO archive on 2026-09-17 matched 144 of them, 145,077 rows across the whole archive rather than this telescope alone; the largest instruments are APEXHET (51456), APEXBOL (26625), VISIR (14125). Adaptive-optics imaging of main-belt asteroids with SPHERE and NAOS+CONICA is the part that could give unphotographed bodies a surface.
entries.revisitWhen: A candidate from the screen is taken up, or the screen is rerun per telescope.
